## Post 1 — hook  📎 fig2_inside_outside.png (TO BUILD)

Reward hacking isn't a morality tale about "deceptive AIs." In our
environment it's a capability race: the policy that searches vs the judge
that scores.

Let search run to saturation and hack rate lands at either 0.97 or 0.06 —
decided by ONE property of the judge. 🧵

> **Alt text (planned fig2)**: Two dots: saturated hack rate 0.971 when the
> judge's blind-spot trap is its global optimum (50 runs) vs 0.056 when it
> is not (300 runs), Mann–Whitney p=1.6e-35. §2 of the writeup.

## Post 2 — the setup

The setup: an environment with a trap — behavior that looks great to a
learned reward model but is actually bad.

The judge: a reward model trained on partial oracle labels. The
contestant: best-of-N search over actions, N from 1 to 1,024.

Hack rate: how often the trap wins.

## Post 3 — the inverted U  📎 fig1_inverted_u.png

Crank up the contestant's search budget and hacking does NOT rise
monotonically.

It rises through mid-range N… then at large N the 50 seeds split into two
populations — and the variance explodes.

The mean is hiding a fork.

> **Alt text**: Line chart titled "More search first inflates hacking, then
> forks the population." Mean hack rate vs best-of-N budget (log scale) for
> the weakest judge: 0.12 at N=1 rising to ~0.76 at N=128, then the ±1 sd
> band balloons (std 0.40 at N=1024) as seeds fork into hack≈1 and hack≈0
> populations.

## Post 4 — the fork, resolved

§2: One property splits the runs — is the trap the global optimum of the
judge's learned scores?

• Trap inside: hack rate 0.971 (0% escape, 0/50)
• Trap outside: 0.056 (75.7% escape, 227/300)

Mann–Whitney p=1.6e-35. Saturated search converges on whatever the judge
loves most.

## Post 5 — the twist

The counterintuitive half: when the trap is NOT the judge's global optimum,
MORE search makes the policy SAFER — big-N search escapes the local trap
that mid-range search gets stuck in.

"Cap the model's optimization pressure" is not automatically the safe
direction here.

## Post 6 — out-of-sample check

§5: We wrote the mechanism down, then ran 50 fresh seeds as an out-of-sample
test.

Prediction: the inside/outside split decides everything.
Result: 0.972 inside vs 0.064 outside (p=2.6e-32), turnover 2.3% vs 78.1%.

The account survived contact with data it wasn't fit on.

## Post 7 — the scaling law

§4: How fast does hacking fall as the judge gets more competent? Slope of
saturated hack rate vs judge competence:

≈ −19, reproduced on three disjoint 50-seed blocks (−18.5 / −19.9 / −19.9,
r² ≥ 0.90).

A 5-point competence gain buys a full swing from always-hack to never-hack.

## Post 8 — corrections we made in public (LONG)

Numbers we corrected along the way, on the record:

• An earlier headline Fisher p=3.96e-42 used a looser "turnover" definition.
The noise-aware recount is p=6.7e-27. Still decisive — but the first number
was the wrong one to lead with.
• A 6-point slope estimate (−14.7) is RETRACTED; the dense 13-point grid and
3-block analysis say ≈ −19.
• An N=1 "control" turned out to be tautological and was dropped.

Densifying the grid shrank the slope's leave-one-out swing from 37–51% to
25%; an endpoint-driven ±12% floor remains. We report "≈ −19", not "−19.9".

## Post 9 — the honest caveats

Caveats:

• One synthetic environment family; "trap" and competence are our
constructs. A mechanism study, not a claim about frontier models.
• Saturated argmax search is an idealization of RL pressure.
• The slope leans on its two endpoints (±12% floor).
• n=50 seeds per block.

## Claims discipline (from threads/README.md — non-negotiable here)

- Lead with saturated hack 0.971/0.056 and MW p=1.6e-35 — NOT the Fisher p.
- Never cite Fisher p=3.96e-42 (looser turnover def) except as the corrected
  item in Post 8; the noise-aware value is 6.7e-27.
- The 6-pt slope −14.7 is retracted; the slope is "≈ −19" (never "−19.9" as
  a headline).
- Do not present the N=1 control as a control.
- No claims about SGPO vs PPO hacking on Murky Drone (refuted; CPO safest).
